clue.text: Fast food once thought to be under threat from Trump?

definitions.text: Fast food once thought to be under threat from Trump?

parts.note: surface reading: quick takeaway grub, burgers and fries of the kind a president is said to love

parts.words: once thought to be under threat from Trump
parts.note: setter's reading: food that is literally fast because it travels by van, a charity service whose funding Trump's first budget was reported to cut

explanation.walkthrough: Trump's appetite for burgers makes 'fast food' look like a junk-food joke; here the food is fast because it moves, delivered by car to elderly people at home.
explanation.definitionFit: The service delivers hot dinners to housebound elderly people, and a 2017 White House budget proposal was widely reported as threatening its federal grants.

clue.text: Incredible Hulk's done for hunters

indicators.note: something incredible cannot be taken at face value, so the letters that follow are not to be read as they stand

parts.note: the possessive is read as plain letters, followed by the word 'done'

explanation.surface: The Incredible Hulk has finished with the people chasing him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Incredible Hulk' reads as the comic-book name, but 'Incredible' is only the signal, and the apostrophe-s supplies an S to the letters being rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Elkhounds are Scandinavian dogs bred for tracking moose, so they are hunting animals, here in the plural to match.

clue.text: Impaler — Vlad's second name in one

indicators.note: 'second' points to the letter in position two of the word it qualifies

parts.note: the second letter of the setter's pseudonym

indicators.note: one thing being in another means it sits inside it, wrapped on both sides

parts.note: an ace is the one in a pack of cards
N is the standard abbreviation for name

explanation.surface: A nod to Vlad the Impaler, the setter joking that his second name is the Impaler.
explanation.walkthrough: The setter's pseudonym Vlad invites thoughts of Vlad the Impaler, so 'Impaler' seems to belong to the name; it is the definition. N goes inside ACE, after the L.
explanation.definitionFit: A lance is a long spear used by mounted knights to pierce opponents, so it is literally an instrument that impales.

clue.text: Maybe obtuse old adult's bored by intellect

parts.note: O is the standard abbreviation for old

indicators.note: something bored by a drill has a hole made through it, so it takes the other piece inside

parts.note: blue films or jokes are adult in the sense of sexually explicit
intelligence quotient, the measure of intellect

explanation.surface: A dim elderly person finds clever talk tedious.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Obtuse' and 'bored' suggest a dull old person, but 'obtuse' is geometry, and 'adult' means explicit, as in blue films. 'Maybe' signals that obtuse is one example of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: In geometry an oblique angle is any angle that is not a right angle, so an obtuse angle is one kind of oblique angle.

clue.text: Glamorgan opener cracking poor delivery to leg — duck!

indicators.note: cracking something means breaking into it, so one piece gets inside another

parts.note: in cricket a wide is a ball bowled out of the batsman's reach, a bad delivery

indicators.note: an opener comes at the start, so only the first letter of the word is wanted

parts.note: the first letter of the Welsh county cricket club
in cricket the leg side is also called the on side

explanation.surface: A Glamorgan opening batsman hits a bad ball down the leg side, and the shout goes up to take cover.
explanation.walkthrough: The cricket scene makes 'duck' look like a score of nought or a shout to take cover; it is the bird. Glamorgan is a Welsh county side, and the leg side in cricket is also called the on side.
explanation.definitionFit: A widgeon, also spelt wigeon, is a dabbling wild duck of Europe and North America with a whistling call.

clue.text: Meet nitpicking accountant British and American separately ignored

indicators.note: things ignored are left out, each one taken away on its own

parts.note: a bean counter is a fussy, penny-pinching accountant
B is the abbreviation for British
A is the abbreviation for American

explanation.surface: Meeting a fussy accountant whose British and American colleagues both snub him.
explanation.walkthrough: The B and the A are removed from separate places in the phrase, which is why 'separately' is there: the B is the first letter and the A sits in the middle.
explanation.definitionFit: To encounter someone is to come across them face to face, a straightforward synonym of the verb meet.

clue.text: Drunk bishop lost gambling game

indicators.note: something lost has gone missing, so it is taken out of the word

parts.note: blotto is slang for very drunk
B is the chess abbreviation for bishop

explanation.surface: A tipsy bishop loses money on a game of chance.
explanation.walkthrough: BLOTTO without its B is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Lotto is a lottery or bingo-like game in which players bet on numbers drawn at random, so it counts as gambling.

clue.text: Charge for coition, pet — Mrs Trump's economic policy

indicators.note: to charge is to rush in violently, an attack that scatters whatever stands in the way

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone asks their partner to pay for sex, addressing her as Mrs Trump.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mrs Trump' looks like a reference to Melania, but MRS is fodder and the apostrophe-s belongs to Trump in the definition. All thirteen letters of the three words are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Protectionism means shielding domestic industry with import tariffs, which is the central plank of Donald Trump's trade agenda.

clue.text: Annoyed by Band-Aid, could be TV Paul's subject matter

definitions.text: could be TV Paul's subject matter

parts.note: cross means irritated or annoyed
a Band-Aid is a sticking plaster, a kind of wound dressing

explanation.surface: Someone irritated by Band Aid, the 1984 charity single, which might be material for a television presenter.
explanation.walkthrough: TV is the abbreviation for transvestite as well as television, so 'TV Paul' is both a television host and a drag performer such as Paul O'Grady, who presented as Lily Savage.
explanation.definitionFit: Wearing clothes of the opposite sex is what a transvestite does, so it would be the natural topic for a drag artiste named Paul.

clue.text: Leftie carrying reading matter is excited again

indicators.note: a thing carrying another holds it within, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: a red is a left-winger or communist
Amazon's Kindle is a device for reading e-books

explanation.surface: A left-winger toting a book or paper is fired up once more.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reading matter' sounds like a book or magazine, but it is the brand name of an e-reader.
explanation.definitionFit: To rekindle is literally to light a fire again, and figuratively to arouse a feeling or interest anew, so it means stirred up once more.

clue.text: Prettier hair-stylist somewhat disheartened

indicators.note: losing part of its heart means some of the middle of the word is removed

parts.note: a hairdresser cuts hair, so is a cutter

explanation.surface: A hairdresser looks better, though a little downcast.
explanation.walkthrough: CUTTER has a double T at its centre; 'somewhat' means only one of those two letters is dropped, not the whole heart.
explanation.definitionFit: Cute means attractive in an endearing way, so its comparative form matches the comparative adjective given in the clue.

clue.text: 'Shark eating raw beginner' could be metaphor

indicators.note: whatever eats something takes it inside itself

parts.note: the tope is a small shark of European waters

indicators.note: a beginner is what starts something, so only the opening letter of the word is wanted

parts.note: the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: A headline about a shark devouring a novice, which might be read as a figure of speech.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Raw beginner' looks like a single phrase for a novice; it is the letter that begins 'raw'. The quotation marks make the whole phrase sound like an example sentence.
explanation.definitionFit: A trope is any figure of speech using words in a non-literal sense, and metaphor is the classic example, hence 'could be'.

clue.text: Unfinished line awful — writer finally stops complaining

indicators.note: something unfinished lacks its end, so the final letter is cut off each word
a stopper plugs a gap, so this piece is pushed into the other

parts.note: a queue is a line of people, here missing its last letter
lousy means awful, also missing its last letter

indicators.note: 'finally' asks for the last letter only

parts.note: the last letter of the word

explanation.surface: A writer abandons a bad line at last and stops grumbling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unfinished' trims both QUEUE and LOUSY; then R is plugged between the E and the U of QUEU, giving QUERULOUS.
explanation.definitionFit: Querulous describes someone who habitually whines and grumbles, an adjective matching the participle used adjectivally.

clue.text: He wouldn't fight against non-feminine boss

indicators.note: 'non-' removes the abbreviation for feminine from the word that follows

parts.note: con means against, as in pros and cons
a chief is a boss, here losing its F

explanation.surface: A man refuses to take on a boss who is not a woman.
explanation.walkthrough: F is the abbreviation for feminine. CONCHIE is British slang, short for conscientious objector.
explanation.definitionFit: A conscientious objector refuses military service on moral grounds; the nickname was common in Britain in both world wars.

clue.text: He helped one going round before fellows left

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: something going is departing, so that letter leaves the word

parts.note: aided means helped
I is the Roman numeral one
O is round in shape
F is the abbreviation for fellow, doubled for the plural

explanation.surface: A man helped someone dizzy before his companions departed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One going round' looks like a single idea, a spinning person; 'one going' removes I from AIDED, and 'round' starts the next chunk.
explanation.definitionFit: To head off is a phrasal verb meaning to set out or depart, so the past tense matches the verb left.

clue.text: Saw what plain cake was?

definitions.meaning: second meaning, split in two: a plain cake has no topping, so it was not covered in frosting

explanation.walkthrough: The second reading splits the answer into two words, NOT ICED, describing a cake without a sugar topping.
explanation.definitionFit: To notice something is to see or become aware of it, so the past tense is an ordinary synonym of the verb saw.

clue.text: Cleaner turned around to catch a bus

parts.note: a char, or charwoman, is a cleaning lady

indicators.note: something turned faces the other way, so these letters run backwards

parts.note: C is short for circa, Latin for around
to nab is to catch
taken as written

explanation.surface: A cleaning lady spun round to hop on a bus.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turned around' looks like one phrase meaning reversed, but 'around' supplies C; only the three pieces after CHAR are turned.
explanation.definitionFit: A charabanc is an old-fashioned open motor coach used for day trips, so it is an early kind of bus.

clue.text: Flash wearing leather in street

parts.note: to be in a coat is to be wearing it

indicators.note: one thing in another sits inside it

parts.note: St is the abbreviation for street
to tan is to make hide into leather, and tan is a leather colour

explanation.surface: Someone flashy in leather gear out on the street.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flash' looks like the British adjective for showy, which fits the leather; it is the noun for a moment.
explanation.definitionFit: In a flash means in a moment, so a flash and an instant are both a very brief interval of time.

clue.text: Where to drive taking gangster to centre of Sleaford — not an honest person

indicators.note: to take something in is to hold it within, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: golfers drive off from the tee
Al Capone, the archetypal gangster

indicators.note: the centre is the middle, so only the middle letters of the word are kept

parts.note: the two middle letters of the Lincolnshire town's name

explanation.surface: Directions for driving a mobster into Sleaford, a market town in Lincolnshire, before a warning about a crook.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Where to drive' points at roads, but the drive is a golf shot. TEA LEAF is Cockney rhyming slang for thief.
explanation.definitionFit: Rhyming slang turns thief into tea leaf, and a thief is by definition dishonest, so the answer is a slang synonym.

clue.text: Choice of routes east round perimeter of Sahara Desert

indicators.note: to go round something is to surround it, holding it inside

parts.note: a fork in the road offers a choice of ways
E is the compass abbreviation for east

indicators.note: a perimeter is the outer edge, so only the outside letters of the word are kept

parts.note: the first and last letters of the word

explanation.surface: Planning which way to go east around the edge of the Sahara Desert.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sahara Desert' reads as one place name, but 'Desert' is the definition, a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To forsake someone is to abandon them, the same as the verb desert, as when a soldier deserts his post.

clue.text: Bucket shape made by French-American corporation

parts.note: Fr is the abbreviation for French
US for American
corporation is old slang for a pot belly, and tum is a belly

explanation.surface: A bucket design produced by a Franco-American company.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Corporation' looks like a company, but it is jocular old slang for a large stomach.
explanation.definitionFit: A frustum is a cone with its top sliced off parallel to the base, which is exactly the tapering profile of a pail.

clue.text: Horror film star, one you said flipped over female

indicators.note: to flip over is to lose control and go wild, so the letters are thrown into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

indicators.note: something said is spoken, so the letter is chosen for how the word is pronounced

parts.note: the letter U is pronounced like the pronoun
F is the abbreviation for female

explanation.surface: Gossip about a horror film actress whom you said went crazy over a woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Horror film star' wants to be one phrase for the definition, but the definition stops at 'film' and 'star' is fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Nosferatu is F. W. Murnau's 1922 silent vampire picture, remade by Herzog and by Eggers, so it is a famous horror movie.

clue.text: United supporters upset — it's a cock-up!

indicators.note: in a down clue, something upset is turned upside down, so the letters read from the bottom up

parts.note: U is the abbreviation for United, as in football club names
fans are supporters of a team

explanation.surface: Manchester United's followers are annoyed at a blunder.
explanation.walkthrough: SNAFU is army slang, an acronym for 'situation normal, all fouled up'; a cock-up is British slang for a botched job.
explanation.definitionFit: A snafu is a chaotic muddle or blunder, exactly what a cock-up means; the definition is phrased as an exclamation.

clue.text: See queens's backside? That's vulgar

indicators.note: the word is used only for its pronunciation, which matches the name of a letter

parts.note: the letter C is pronounced like the verb
R stands for Regina, Latin for queen
ass is American slang for the bottom

explanation.surface: Someone mooned the drag queens, and that is in poor taste.
explanation.walkthrough: 'See' is not looking here; it stands for the letter with the same sound, and R is the regnal abbreviation for a queen.
explanation.definitionFit: Crass means grossly insensitive and lacking refinement, which is a close synonym of coarse or vulgar behaviour.

clue.text: Nurse having no time for president

indicators.note: having none of something means it has been removed from the word

parts.note: Jimmy Carter, 39th president of the United States
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: A nurse too busy to attend to the president.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove T from CARTER.
explanation.definitionFit: A carer looks after a sick, elderly or disabled person, much as a nurse tends patients, so the nouns are close synonyms.

clue.text: Has clocked stunner in hat

indicators.note: a clock hand goes round in a circle, so the letters rotate, the end coming round to the front

parts.note: taken as written
a KO, or knockout, is a blow that stuns

explanation.surface: Someone has noticed a gorgeous person wearing a hat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clocked' looks like British slang for noticed or for punching; it sends the last letter of HAS round to the front, and 'stunner' is a knockout, not a beauty.
explanation.definitionFit: A shako is a tall cylindrical military cap with a peak and a plume, worn by soldiers in the nineteenth century.

clue.text: Please, what can you do in Victoria? One right to leave

indicators.note: whatever leaves goes away, so it is taken out of the phrase

parts.words: what can you do in Victoria?
parts.note: Victoria is a London railway station, where you can get on a train
R for right; only one of the two in the phrase goes

explanation.surface: Someone asking what activities are available in the Australian state of Victoria.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Victoria' suggests the Australian state or the queen, but it is the London terminus: ENTER TRAIN drops one of its two Rs, the one in TRAIN.
explanation.definitionFit: To entertain an audience is to amuse and delight it, and to please someone is to give them enjoyment, so the verbs match.

clue.text: If camouflager's clever, some may not recognise its existence

definitions.text: some may not recognise its existence

indicators.note: a clever disguise artist rearranges things deftly, so the letters are craftily reworked

parts.note: taken as written, thirteen letters

explanation.surface: If a master of disguise is good enough, some people will not even notice he exists.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is about camouflage making something invisible; the letters of 'If camouflager' are the fodder. In 2025 Trump renamed the Gulf of Mexico by executive order, a name much of the world ignores.
explanation.definitionFit: Outside US federal usage, most countries and many publications still call the body of water the Gulf of Mexico, refusing the new name.
